q1: SELECT b.name AS bar, COUNT(DISTINCT f.drinker) AS num_drinker, AVG(s.price) AS avg_price, (SELECT f1.drinker FROM frequents AS f1 WHERE f1.bar = b.name ORDER BY f1.times_a_week DESC, f1.drinker ASC LIMIT 1) AS most_reg_drinker FROM bar AS b LEFT JOIN frequents AS f ON b.name = f.bar LEFT JOIN serves AS s ON b.name = s.bar GROUP BY b.name ORDER BY num_drinker DESC, b.name ASC
q2: SELECT G.bar, COALESCE(COUNT(DISTINCT G.drinker), 0) AS num_of_drinkers, COALESCE(AVG(price), NULL) AS average, COALESCE((SELECT drinker FROM frequents WHERE bar = G.bar ORDER BY times_a_week DESC, drinker LIMIT 1), NULL) FROM serves NATURAL JOIN frequents AS g GROUP BY G.bar ORDER BY SUM(G.times_a_week) DESC, G.bar

explanation: Q1 and Q2 are not semantically equivalent because Q1 uses a subquery to find the most regular drinker for each bar, while Q2 uses a correlated subquery to achieve the same result. The difference arises when there are ties in the number of times a drinker visits a bar in a week. Q1 will return the drinker with the lexicographically smallest name in case of a tie, while Q2 will return the drinker with the highest number of visits in case of a tie.
counterexample_dsp: Create a scenario where two drinkers visit a bar the same number of times a week, and their names are lexicographically different. Q1 should return the drinker with the lexicographically smaller name, while Q2 should return the drinker with the higher number of visits.
